title: Kumbha and the burned hut
hookLine: a king bows to a young teacher, never guessing it's his wife
carry: tyaga: give up the grip, not just the things
tomorrow: the king is free, alone in a hut. what does a free person do next?

lines: A BARE ROOM, A FREE MIND?
cards: Decluttering videos make a promise: a bare room means a free mind. Give away the stuff, and the weight goes with it. King Shikhidhvaja tried a version of that.
He left a kingdom for a forest hut. Then a young Brahmin walks in, who calls himself Kumbha. The king bows to him as a teacher, never guessing it's Chudala, his own wife, in disguise.
She's come to teach the husband who wouldn't hear her at home. Her first question: have you really given up everything?

teach.b: Two views of giving up meet in that hut. The king's view: renunciation means leaving things behind. He has paid for it: kingdom, wealth, palace, wife.
It isn't foolish. Leaving things behind is real work, and he did it with his whole heart. Kumbha's view: something is still left.

teach.h: THE HUT, THE STAFF, THE BOWL, BURNED.
teach.b: So the king looks at what remains, his hut, his staff, his bowl, and he burns them and watches them go. Now?

teach.h: KUMBHA: THE GRIP IS STILL THERE.
teach.b: Still not everything, Kumbha says. What's left was never a thing. It's the one doing the holding: the mind that clings, the sense of mine and I.

teach.h: GIVE UP THE GRIP, NOT JUST THE THINGS.
teach.b: Give that up, Kumbha says, and you've given up everything. The Sanskrit word is tyaga, renunciation, and the Bhagavad Gita uses it the same way: tyaga is letting go of the clinging to results, not of the work.
And Kumbha doesn't call the king's way wrong. She says it isn't finished. One view moves outward, one thing at a time, and something is always left.
The other turns inward, to the grip itself. Vasistha tells this to Rama, a prince who wanted to walk away from the world, about a king who walked away and was still holding on.

how: Hindu tradition honors both kinds of giving up: some take sannyasa and leave home, while householders are taught to act without clinging; teachers often tell Chudala's story to show the second.

o: a story where a queen burns a palace to punish a king
a sage's story where giving up the grip is giving up all
a story where a king wins back his throne from a rival

games.q: in the forest hut — tap the pairs.
p: Chudala in disguise, a young teacher
the grip: the sense of mine and I

s: renouncing everything means owning nothing at all
the king burned his last things and still hadn't; the clinging mind was left.
Kumbha is Chudala, the king's wife, in disguise
she comes to teach the husband who wouldn't hear her at home.
Kumbha mocks the king for leaving his kingdom
she says his giving up isn't finished, not that it was foolish.

games.q: two friends argue about a phone break. one says delete the apps, it's the only real way. the other says the problem is the grip, not the phone. what's the first friend's best case?
o: leaving things behind is real work, and it clears the way.
phones are bad, so anyone who keeps one is weak.
nothing you do changes anything, so delete them.
games.why: the king's way is honest work, and Kumbha doesn't mock it. she only says it isn't finished: the grip itself is still left.

practice: Pick up something small you'd hate to lose: a ring, your keys, your phone. Hold it tightly in your fist for a few breaths and feel the grip.
Then open your hand slowly, so it rests on your open palm, still yours and still there, with only the clutching gone.

wordCard.voice: The Yoga Vasistha: here, Kumbha's tyaga, giving up not the things but the grip on them.

orig.note: Sanskrit tyaga: giving up, renunciation; in Kumbha's teaching, giving up the grip.

carryVoice: Your line: tyaga, give up the grip, not just the things. Burn the hut, and the grip can still be there. Sixteen-oh-six, done.

sources.ref: Yoga Vasistha, Nirvana Prakarana (the story of Chudala and Shikhidhvaja: Chudala as Kumbha; the king burning his possessions; Kumbha's teaching that renouncing all is renouncing the clinging mind)
Bhagavad Gita 18.2 (tyaga as giving up the fruits of all actions)
